rows.reason: The round-4 miscite is fixed and every citation now checks: the leaver's cardigan is across lines 13 and 14 ('a girl who had left in Year Four' / 'put it in the returns box anyway.'); 'Friday box' is on line 33; 'It won't fit me next year.' is on line 47; 'longer than the answer needed' is on line 48; 'September football trials' is on line 38. All quotations are word for word, the script has 5 sentences of 16, 9, 15, 15 and 14 words, there is no first person, and the key comes only at the end, after the evidence. The key is still the one defensible answer. The new first sentence fails on readability and on teaching, though: 'Lines 13 and 14 return a leaver's cardigan; his jumper goes in line 33's "Friday box".' The point of this sentence is the CONTRAST: he keeps a stranger's cardigan to be returned, yet gives away his own jumper. Round 4 marked that with 'but'. The semicolon removes it, so a 9-11-year-old gets two unlinked facts and has to work out the relation alone. That relation is the whole step. The sentence also packs two line references, a possessive on a line number ('line 33's') and lines as the subject that does the returning ('Lines 13 and 14 return') into one semicolon-joined sentence. That is too dense for this age group. Fix: split it into two plain sentences with the contrast word kept, e.g. 'In lines 13 and 14 he returns a cardigan whose owner has left.' / 'Yet on line 33 his own jumper goes in "the Friday box".' To stay within 5 sentences, merge the last two, e.g. 'He is giving up next year, so the trials sheet has a space he will not fill.' (16 words; line 38's 'September football trials' may then be cited in the sentence about Miss Bhatt or dropped, since the stem already points to lines 37 to 39). The other sentences need no change. The fault is in the script, not the question.
